factStatement: Assignment stores the value on the right into the name on the left; it is not a statement of equality.
familyName: Reading an assignment in the right direction
measurementObjective: Say which name changes and which value it takes, given a single assignment.
distractorStrategy: The assignment read right-to-left; both names claimed to change; the assignment read as asserting the two are now permanently equal. The last is the belief that later makes x = x + 1 look impossible.
notes: Show real code in the stem. x = y is the whole item; no scenario is needed and none should be added.

factStatement: Every value has a type, and the type is visible in how the value is written.
familyName: Naming the type of a written value
measurementObjective: Given literals as they appear in code, name each type.
distractorStrategy: The productive cases are "5" against 5, 5 against 5.0, and True against "True". A student who reads past the quotes gets all three wrong, which is exactly the confusion that breaks input handling later.
notes: Quoted digits must appear in every variant.

factStatement: An output statement displays a value and changes nothing else.
familyName: What one output statement produces
measurementObjective: Give exactly what a single output statement prints.
distractorStrategy: The variable name printed rather than its value; the value with quotes where there are none; the value the variable held before the preceding assignment.
notes: The D1 entry point for the skill. One or two lines only.

factStatement: Assignment stores the value on the right into the name on the left; it is not a statement of equality.
familyName: Tracing one variable through several assignments
measurementObjective: Give the value a named variable holds after a short run of assignments where order matters.
distractorStrategy: The first value assigned rather than the last; the value from the line before the one asked about; the result of applying the assignments in written order to the wrong variable.
notes: Same fact as PGF_FAM01, different measurement: that one is answerable from a definition, this one only by tracing. Same reassessment group so they are never served together.

factStatement: An expression is evaluated to a single value before it is stored or displayed.
familyName: Evaluating an expression to its value
measurementObjective: Give the value an expression produces, including its type.
distractorStrategy: The right number as the wrong type; the operands combined in written order ignoring precedence; the expression left unevaluated as text.

factStatement: Operator precedence decides the order of evaluation, and brackets override it.
familyName: Working out which operation happens first
measurementObjective: Evaluate an expression whose result depends on precedence, or choose the bracketing that gives a stated result.
distractorStrategy: Strict left-to-right evaluation — the answer that reveals precedence has not landed. Also the correct precedence with one operator misread, and a bracketing that changes the result in the other direction.
notes: The expression must give different answers under left-to-right and under precedence, or the item measures arithmetic instead.

factStatement: Every value has a type, and the type is visible in how the value is written.
familyName: How type changes what an operator does
measurementObjective: Predict the result of the same operator applied to different types.
distractorStrategy: "5" + "5" answered as 10 — the single most valuable distractor in this skill. Also numeric addition where concatenation happens, and an error claimed where the operation is perfectly legal.
notes: Same fact as PGF_FAM02: that one names types, this one shows why naming them matters.

factStatement: Input arrives as text and must be converted before it can be used as a number.
familyName: Reasoning about unconverted input
measurementObjective: Predict what happens when input is used without conversion, and what conversion is needed.
distractorStrategy: Arithmetic succeeding on unconverted input; concatenation of two inputs reported as a sum (the classic "2" + "3" giving "23"); a crash where the language quietly concatenates instead.
notes: This family catches the single commonest first-program bug. Worth several items.

factStatement: Statements run in order, and reordering them can change the result.
familyName: How reordering statements changes the outcome
measurementObjective: Given two orderings of the same statements, say whether the results differ and how.
distractorStrategy: Claiming the orders are equivalent when they are not; claiming they differ when the statements are genuinely independent. Include one pair that IS equivalent, or the family teaches that order always matters.

factStatement: Division, integer division and remainder are different operations and give different results.
familyName: Distinguishing the division operators
measurementObjective: Give the result of each division-family operator on the same operands.
distractorStrategy: The float answer where integer division was used and the reverse; the remainder where the quotient was asked; a rounded result where truncation happens. Negative operands are the D4 case and separate rule-following from memory.
notes: Foundation-critical rather than trivia: this is where counting and averaging code silently goes wrong.

factStatement: A program can refuse to run, stop while running, or run to completion and be wrong; these are different failures.
familyName: Classifying how a program failed
measurementObjective: Given a fragment and what happened, classify the failure and say when it was detected.
distractorStrategy: A logic error reported as a crash; a runtime failure attributed to syntax; the claim that a program producing output cannot be wrong. The last is the belief this family exists to break.

factStatement: Using a variable before anything has been stored in it fails; initialising it in the wrong place has the same effect.
familyName: Diagnosing a missing or misplaced initialisation
measurementObjective: Identify why a fragment fails or gives a wrong total, given where its variables are initialised.
distractorStrategy: Blame the arithmetic rather than the initialisation; blame the input; propose an initialisation in a position that would still be wrong. The accumulator initialised inside a loop is the canonical stem.

factStatement: Copying one variable into another does not link them; changing one afterwards leaves the other alone.
familyName: Tracing several interacting variables
measurementObjective: Give the values of all named variables after a fragment where one is copied and then changed.
distractorStrategy: Both variables updated as though linked; the swap performed without the temporary so one value is lost; the values from one step earlier. A three-variable rotation is the D5 case.
notes: Swap-without-temporary is the highest-value stem here and belongs in most variants.

factStatement: Zero, negative, empty and boundary inputs are where a fragment that works on ordinary values stops working.
familyName: Predicting behaviour on an extreme input
measurementObjective: Say what a fragment does on zero, negative or empty input.
distractorStrategy: The answer for ordinary input; a crash where the code quietly returns something wrong; a wrong value where it genuinely does crash. Distinguishing a quiet wrong answer from a failure is the measurement.
notes: Division by a computed zero is the canonical D5 stem: the zero must be arrived at, not written.

factStatement: Two fragments written differently can behave identically, and two written similarly can not.
familyName: Judging whether two fragments behave the same
measurementObjective: Decide whether two fragments produce the same result for every input, and name the input that separates them if not.
distractorStrategy: A pair differing only at a boundary; a pair differing only on empty input; a pair that genuinely is equivalent despite looking different. Every option must be plausible on typical input.
notes: The separating input must exist and be findable. If no input distinguishes them, the answer is "equivalent" and the item still works.

factStatement: Python literals carry their type in how they are written: 5, 5.0, "5" and True are four different values.
familyName: Naming a Python literal type
measurementObjective: Name the type of each of several Python literals shown in code.
distractorStrategy: "5" called an int, 5.0 called an int, True called a string. All three come from reading the value and ignoring how it is written.

factStatement: print displays the value of what it is given, without the quotes of a string literal.
familyName: What a single print produces
measurementObjective: Give exactly what one or two print statements output.
distractorStrategy: Output shown with quotes; the variable name printed instead of its value; two prints shown on one line when they produce two.
notes: Whether the output occupies one line or two is a real distinction and worth measuring.

factStatement: A Python name may contain letters, digits and underscores but may not begin with a digit, and case matters.
familyName: Deciding whether a name is usable
measurementObjective: Identify which of several names Python accepts.
distractorStrategy: A name beginning with a digit; one containing a hyphen; two names differing only in case treated as the same. The case pair is the one that matters, because it causes real bugs rather than a refusal to run.
notes: Admitted as Foundation-critical rather than trivia: a beginner blocked by an invalid name cannot proceed at all.

factStatement: Assigning to a name again replaces what it referred to, whatever the type of either value.
familyName: Tracing Python assignments
measurementObjective: Give what a name refers to after a short sequence of assignments, including one that changes type.
distractorStrategy: The earlier value; an error claimed for the type change (Python permits it, and believing otherwise is a real misconception); the two values combined.

factStatement: String positions start at zero, and a negative index counts from the end.
familyName: Indexing into a string
measurementObjective: Give the character or slice a given index or slice expression produces.
distractorStrategy: One-based indexing; the slice end treated as inclusive; a negative index counted from the wrong end. Off-by-one is the whole family.

factStatement: String methods return a new string and leave the original unchanged.
familyName: What a string method returns and what it leaves
measurementObjective: Give the result of a string method call, and say what the original variable holds afterwards.
distractorStrategy: The original reported as modified in place — the misconception this family exists for. Also the wrong case for a case-changing method, and whitespace not removed where strip was called. Options must preserve case exactly: the case IS the answer.
notes: A case-sensitivity item cannot have its options compared case-insensitively anywhere in the pipeline.

factStatement: A list can be changed in place, and two names can refer to the same list.
familyName: Reasoning about a changed list
measurementObjective: Give the contents of each named list after an in-place change, where two names may refer to one list.
distractorStrategy: The second name treated as an independent copy — the central misconception. Also the change applied to the wrong position, and an error claimed where mutation is legal.
notes: The aliasing case is the D4 measurement and should not be diluted with plain indexing variants.

factStatement: input always returns a string, whatever the user typed.
familyName: Reasoning about the type input returns
measurementObjective: Predict the result of arithmetic or comparison on a value taken straight from input.
distractorStrategy: Numeric addition of two inputs reported as a sum rather than a concatenation; a comparison against a number reported as working; a crash where concatenation quietly succeeds.

factStatement: Converting a string to a number succeeds only if the text is a number.
familyName: What conversion does and when it fails
measurementObjective: Say what a conversion produces for given text, including when it fails.
distractorStrategy: int("3.5") reported as 3 rather than failing — the most instructive case. Also a failure claimed for text that converts fine, and a float conversion reported as truncating.

factStatement: In Python / gives a float, // truncates toward negative infinity, and % gives a remainder.
familyName: Distinguishing /, // and %
measurementObjective: Give the result and type of each division-family operator on the same operands.
distractorStrategy: 7 / 2 reported as 3; 7 // 2 reported as 3.5; the remainder confused with the quotient. Negative operands are the D4 case, since -7 // 2 is not -3.
notes: The float result of / is Python-specific and catches students transferring from C.

factStatement: Zero, the empty string and the empty list are false in a condition; other values of those types are true.
familyName: Deciding the truth value of a non-boolean
measurementObjective: Say whether a condition holds when the value tested is not a boolean.
distractorStrategy: An error claimed for testing a non-boolean; zero treated as true because it exists; the string "False" treated as false. The last is a genuine and common confusion.

factStatement: Indexing beyond the end of a sequence fails; the last valid index is one less than the length.
familyName: Diagnosing an out-of-range access
measurementObjective: Identify why an access fails and what the largest valid index was.
distractorStrategy: The length given as the last valid index; the failure blamed on the value rather than the position; a loop bound reported as safe when it reaches the length.

factStatement: A fragment combining assignment, a condition and a loop produces one determinate output.
familyName: Tracing a fragment that combines several constructs
measurementObjective: Give the printed output of a short fragment using assignment, a condition and a loop together.
distractorStrategy: The result of one extra or one fewer iteration; the value printed before the final update; the answer from taking the other branch. Each distractor must be reachable by one identifiable slip.
notes: The strongest family in the skill: it cannot be answered without tracing. D5 uses an unfamiliar combination rather than more lines.

factStatement: An empty string or list makes loops run zero times and makes some operations fail.
familyName: Behaviour on an empty sequence
measurementObjective: Say what a fragment does when its sequence is empty.
distractorStrategy: The loop assumed to run once; an initialised accumulator reported as an error; a crash where the code returns the initial value quietly. The last is the most instructive, since a silent zero is worse than a failure.
notes: Averaging an empty list is the canonical stem: it separates a quiet wrong answer from a division failure.

factStatement: Two expressions can give the same result on some inputs and differ on others.
familyName: Judging whether two expressions always agree
measurementObjective: Decide whether two expressions agree for every input, and name a value where they differ.
distractorStrategy: Pairs that agree on positive integers and differ on zero, on negatives, or between int and float. Every option must look interchangeable at a glance.

factStatement: Each comparison operator has a precise meaning, and the ones including equality differ from the ones excluding it.
familyName: Reading a comparison operator
measurementObjective: Say whether a given comparison is true for stated values, including at the boundary.
distractorStrategy: Strict and inclusive swapped at the boundary; == confused with =; a comparison reported as an error. Every variant should include equal operands, since that is where the operators separate.
notes: Equal operands must appear, or the item cannot distinguish < from <=.

factStatement: A condition evaluates to true or false, and that value can be stored like any other.
familyName: Recognising a boolean result
measurementObjective: Identify what a comparison produces and what type it is.
distractorStrategy: The comparison reported as producing one of its operands; the result as the string "True"; the claim that a comparison cannot be stored.

factStatement: Exactly one branch of an if/else runs, and code after the conditional runs either way.
familyName: Identifying which lines are inside a branch
measurementObjective: Given an indented fragment, say which lines run conditionally and which always run.
distractorStrategy: A line after the conditional treated as part of the last branch — the indentation misreading that causes real bugs. Also both branches claimed to run, and neither.
notes: Show indentation exactly. This family measures reading structure, so the structure must be visible.

factStatement: A condition is evaluated against the current values of its variables.
familyName: Evaluating a condition on given values
measurementObjective: Say whether a condition holds for stated variable values.
distractorStrategy: Evaluation against the values before an intervening assignment; the comparison reversed; a boundary sent the wrong way.

factStatement: Exactly one branch of an if/else runs, and code after the conditional runs either way.
familyName: Deciding which branch runs and what it prints
measurementObjective: Give the output of a conditional fragment for stated input.
distractorStrategy: The other branch taken; both branches printed; the code after the conditional omitted. Include boundary input in most variants.
notes: Same fact as CB_FAM03, different measurement: that one reads structure, this one runs it.

factStatement: else runs when no earlier condition held, and an if with no else may run nothing at all.
familyName: What happens when no condition holds
measurementObjective: Say what a fragment does for input that satisfies none of its conditions.
distractorStrategy: The first branch assumed to run as a default; an error claimed for an if with no else; the last branch treated as a catch-all when it has its own condition.

factStatement: In a chain, conditions are tested in order and the first true one wins, so reordering changes the result.
familyName: How the order of a chain changes the outcome
measurementObjective: Say which branch a value reaches in a chain, and what reordering would change.
distractorStrategy: A later branch reached although an earlier condition also held — the misconception that all matching branches run. Also a reordering claimed harmless when it changes the result for overlapping ranges.
notes: Overlapping ranges are essential; a chain of disjoint conditions cannot measure order.

factStatement: and requires both parts, or requires either, and not inverts.
familyName: Evaluating a combined condition
measurementObjective: Say whether a combined condition holds for stated values.
distractorStrategy: and and or swapped; not applied to the wrong part; a condition true for one part reported as true overall under and. The D4 case negates a combined condition, where students distribute not incorrectly.

factStatement: Whether a boundary value is included depends on whether the operator includes equality.
familyName: What happens exactly at the boundary
measurementObjective: Say what a fragment does for input exactly equal to its threshold.
distractorStrategy: The behaviour just below or just above the boundary; the boundary assumed included; a gap where two conditions both exclude it. The uncovered-boundary case is the most valuable.
notes: This family carries the most weight in the skill: nearly every real conditional bug is a boundary.

factStatement: An inner condition is only reached when the outer one held.
familyName: Tracing nested conditions
measurementObjective: Give the output of a nested conditional for stated input.
distractorStrategy: The inner branch reached although the outer failed; the inner else attached to the outer if; the output for the sibling case. Indentation must be exact and must matter.

factStatement: A rule stated in words determines exactly one correct condition, including at its boundary.
familyName: Choosing the condition that implements a rule
measurementObjective: Given a rule in words, choose the condition that implements it exactly.
distractorStrategy: Strict where inclusive was meant; the comparison reversed; a condition correct for typical values and wrong at the edge. "At least" and "more than" in the rule text are the discriminators.

factStatement: A conditional that gives the wrong answer for particular inputs points to a specific fault in its conditions.
familyName: Finding the fault from which inputs are wrong
measurementObjective: Given a fragment and the inputs it handles wrongly, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: Faults that would produce a different wrong set; correct parts of the condition; the input blamed rather than the condition. The set of failing inputs must implicate exactly one fault.
notes: Stating WHICH inputs are wrong is what makes this diagnosis rather than inspection.

factStatement: A branch can be impossible to reach because an earlier condition already covers every value that would satisfy it.
familyName: Spotting a branch that can never run
measurementObjective: Identify which branch of a chain is unreachable and why.
distractorStrategy: A branch that is merely rare; one reachable only at a boundary; the claim that all branches are reachable. Requires reasoning over the whole chain, not one line.

factStatement: Two differently written conditions can select exactly the same values, or differ only at an edge.
familyName: Judging whether two conditions select the same values
measurementObjective: Decide whether two conditions are equivalent, and name a value that separates them if not.
distractorStrategy: A pair differing only at the boundary; a negation distributed incorrectly over and/or; a pair that genuinely is equivalent. All options must look interchangeable.
notes: De Morgan without naming it: not (a and b) against (not a) or (not b) is the canonical D5 pair.

factStatement: A loop runs its body more than once instead of the code being written out repeatedly.
familyName: Recognising what a loop replaces
measurementObjective: Identify which repeated code a loop replaces, or which task needs one.
distractorStrategy: A task with a fixed, known number of distinct steps offered as needing a loop; a loop claimed to run its body once; a conditional offered as repetition.

conceptName: The values a loop runs over
factStatement: A range from 0 to n produces n values, ending one before n.
familyName: Listing the values a range produces
measurementObjective: Give the values a stated range yields.
distractorStrategy: The end value included; counting from one; n+1 values. Inclusion of the end is the entire measurement and every distractor should turn on it.
notes: The one fact that, misunderstood, makes every subsequent loop item wrong.

factStatement: A counted loop suits a known number of repetitions; a conditional loop suits repeating until something becomes true.
familyName: Choosing the kind of loop a task needs
measurementObjective: Given a described repetition, choose the loop form that fits.
distractorStrategy: A counted loop chosen where the count is not known in advance; a conditional loop where the count is fixed; the claim that only one form exists. Keep it about fit, not preference.

conceptName: The values a loop runs over
factStatement: A range from 0 to n produces n values, ending one before n.
familyName: How many times the body runs
measurementObjective: Give the number of times a loop body executes for stated bounds.
distractorStrategy: One too many or one too few; the difference between the bounds where a step is involved; the count of values rather than executions where a break is present.
notes: Same fact as LP_FAM02, applied rather than recalled.

factStatement: The loop variable takes a new value each time round and holds its final value after the loop.
familyName: What the loop variable holds at a given point
measurementObjective: Give the loop variable value during a named iteration and after the loop finishes.
distractorStrategy: The value one iteration out; the end bound rather than the last value taken; the initial value. The after-the-loop case is the productive one.

factStatement: An accumulator adds each value to a running result and must be initialised before the loop.
familyName: What an accumulator holds at the end
measurementObjective: Give the accumulator value after the loop, for stated input.
distractorStrategy: The result of initialising inside the loop, so only the last value survives — the single most valuable distractor. Also the count instead of the total, and the total missing the first or last item.

factStatement: A counter increases by a fixed step each time a condition is met, counting occurrences rather than summing values.
familyName: What a counter holds at the end
measurementObjective: Give the counter value after a loop that counts only matching items.
distractorStrategy: The total of the matching values rather than how many; every item counted regardless of the condition; the count off by one from initialising at one.
notes: A loop needing both a counter and an accumulator — an average — is the strongest D4 stem.

factStatement: A conditional loop stops only when something inside it makes the condition false.
familyName: Reasoning about whether a loop stops
measurementObjective: Decide whether a loop terminates for stated input and what makes it stop.
distractorStrategy: Termination claimed where nothing changes the condition; non-termination claimed where the update is inside a branch that does run; the loop assumed to stop after a fixed number of turns regardless.

factStatement: If the condition is false at entry the body never runs, and whatever it would have set keeps its initial value.
familyName: What happens when the loop does not run
measurementObjective: Give the output of a loop whose condition is false before the first iteration.
distractorStrategy: The body assumed to run once — the misconception this family exists for. Also an error claimed, and the value the loop would have produced had it run.

factStatement: An inner loop runs fully for each iteration of the outer one.
familyName: How many times a nested body runs
measurementObjective: Give the total executions of the inner body, or the output of a nested pair.
distractorStrategy: The bounds added rather than multiplied; the inner loop counted once; the count when the inner bound depends on the outer variable computed as though it were fixed.
notes: A dependent inner bound is the D4 case and much stronger than two fixed bounds.

factStatement: break leaves the loop immediately, skipping the rest of the body and all remaining iterations.
familyName: What break skips
measurementObjective: Give the output of a loop containing a break, for stated input.
distractorStrategy: break treated as skipping one iteration (confusing it with continue) — the central confusion; the rest of the body after break assumed to run; break in a nested loop assumed to leave both.
notes: Foundation-appropriate as behaviour, not as style advice.

factStatement: continue abandons the rest of this iteration and starts the next one.
familyName: What continue skips
measurementObjective: Give the output of a loop containing a continue.
distractorStrategy: continue treated as leaving the loop; the skipped statements assumed to run anyway; a counter after the continue assumed to have been reached. Pairing it with a counter placed after the continue is the strongest stem.

factStatement: A loop that never ends has a condition nothing in the body can make false.
familyName: Finding why a loop never ends
measurementObjective: Identify the line whose absence or placement causes a loop not to terminate.
distractorStrategy: Lines that are correct; an update present but inside a branch that never runs; the condition blamed when the update is the fault. The D5 case makes the update reachable but ineffective.

factStatement: A loop processing one item too many or too few has a bound or a starting value one out.
familyName: Diagnosing an off-by-one from the result
measurementObjective: Given a loop and a result one out from expected, identify what to change.
distractorStrategy: A change that fixes the count but breaks the values; one that moves the error to the other end; a change to the accumulator where the bound is at fault. Several options must plausibly shift the result by one.
notes: The commonest real loop bug, and the one most worth measuring at transfer level.

factStatement: Empty and single-item input are where a loop that works on ordinary input misbehaves.
familyName: Tracing a loop on empty or single-item input
measurementObjective: Say what a loop produces for empty or single-item input.
distractorStrategy: The ordinary-input answer; a failure where the initial value is returned quietly; a value where it genuinely fails. Finding a maximum with the accumulator initialised to zero is the canonical stem, since it returns a plausible wrong answer for all-negative input.

factStatement: A function gives a name to a piece of work so it can be used repeatedly without being rewritten.
familyName: Recognising what a function achieves
measurementObjective: Identify what defining a function gives you that repeating the code does not.
distractorStrategy: A function claimed to make code run faster; claimed to be required by the language; claimed to run on its own once defined. The last is a real belief and leads to confusion about calls.

factStatement: Defining a function does not run it; the body runs only when the function is called.
familyName: Telling a definition from a call
measurementObjective: Say whether a fragment produces output, given that it defines a function and may or may not call it.
distractorStrategy: The body assumed to run at the point of definition — the misconception this family exists for. Also the body assumed to run once per definition and once per call.
notes: A fragment that defines but never calls is the sharpest stem: the correct answer is that nothing is printed.

factStatement: A parameter is the name in the definition; an argument is the value supplied at the call.
familyName: Distinguishing a parameter from an argument
measurementObjective: Given a definition and a call, identify which names are parameters and which values are arguments.
distractorStrategy: The terms swapped; the return value called an argument; a variable outside the function called a parameter. The vocabulary matters because every later error message uses it.

factStatement: A call suspends the caller, runs the body, and resumes the caller where it left off.
familyName: Tracing the order of execution across a call
measurementObjective: Give the order in which output appears when a function is called mid-way through other code.
distractorStrategy: The function output placed first because the definition appears first; the caller output shown entirely before the callee; output ordered by line number rather than by execution.
notes: Definition placed above the call, and output interleaved, so line order and execution order genuinely differ.

factStatement: Arguments are matched to parameters by position, so their order matters.
familyName: Matching arguments to parameters
measurementObjective: Give the result of a call where swapping the arguments would change the answer.
distractorStrategy: The arguments bound in reverse; binding by name similarity rather than position; an error claimed where the call is valid. The operation must be non-commutative, or the swap is undetectable.
notes: Subtraction or division in the body; never addition.

factStatement: return sends a value back to the caller and ends the function immediately.
familyName: What the caller receives
measurementObjective: Give what a call evaluates to, and what happens to code after the return.
distractorStrategy: Code after the return assumed to run; the returned value assumed to be printed; the last computed value returned rather than the one named. A return inside a loop is the D4 case.

factStatement: A function with no return gives back nothing usable, even if it printed something.
familyName: What a function without a return gives back
measurementObjective: Say what the caller receives from a function that prints but does not return.
distractorStrategy: The printed value assumed to be returned — the single most valuable distractor in this skill. Also the last assignment inside the body assumed to be returned, and an error claimed at the point of definition.
notes: The print/return confusion is the defining Foundation error with functions.

factStatement: Each call starts fresh; values from a previous call do not carry over.
familyName: Reasoning about repeated calls
measurementObjective: Give the results of two successive calls to the same function.
distractorStrategy: The second call assumed to continue from the first, so a local counter appears to accumulate; both calls assumed to return the first result; an error claimed on the second call.

factStatement: A name created inside a function exists only while it runs and cannot be used outside.
familyName: What is visible outside a function
measurementObjective: Say whether a name is available after the function returns, and what happens if it is used.
distractorStrategy: The local assumed visible outside; the local assumed to overwrite an outer name of the same name; the value assumed to persist between calls.

factStatement: A parameter or local with the same name as an outer variable is a different variable; changing it leaves the outer one alone.
familyName: Reasoning about two variables with one name
measurementObjective: Give the value of the outer variable after a function that assigns to a same-named local.
distractorStrategy: The outer variable assumed changed — the whole point. Also an error claimed for reusing the name, and the two values assumed to be combined.

factStatement: A function with no return gives back nothing usable, even if it printed something.
familyName: Choosing between returning and printing
measurementObjective: Decide which of two functions can have its result used in a further calculation, and why.
distractorStrategy: The printing version claimed usable because the value was visible; both claimed equivalent; the returning version claimed to print. Show two functions differing only in return versus print.
notes: Same fact as FN_FAM07, at the level of choosing rather than predicting.

factStatement: A long piece of code can be split into functions that each do one nameable thing.
familyName: Choosing a useful split into functions
measurementObjective: Choose the split whose functions each do one thing and together cover the task.
distractorStrategy: A split that leaves part of the task in no function; one whose functions each need the others half-finished; one that splits on line count rather than on responsibility. All options must be syntactically fine, so the judgement is about structure.
notes: Ties back to PS_FAM06. Different skill, so a separate reassessment group by rule; noted here because the two measure related judgement.

factStatement: A function that returns the wrong thing usually has a misplaced return, a shadowed name, or nothing returned at all.
familyName: Diagnosing why a function gives the wrong result
measurementObjective: Given a function and a wrong result, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: A return placed inside a loop so it exits on the first item; a printed value where a return was needed; an outer variable relied on instead of a parameter. Every option must be a real fault pattern, with only one producing the stated symptom.
notes: Return-inside-the-loop is the canonical D5 stem: the function works for single-item input and fails otherwise.

factStatement: A function correct for ordinary arguments can fail or return something wrong for empty, zero or boundary arguments.
familyName: Behaviour of a function on an extreme argument
measurementObjective: Say what a function returns for an empty, zero or boundary argument.
distractorStrategy: The ordinary-argument result; a failure where nothing is returned quietly; a returned value where it genuinely fails. Distinguishing "returns nothing" from "fails" is the measurement.
